input:
Notes - tuition business, parent billing (short call)

- Parents are invoiced monthly for sessions delivered.
- The source of what to bill is each tutor's own session log. Tutors record sessions somewhere - a shared sheet was mentioned, but also "some of them just message me".
- Who compiles the invoices was not established. The answer given was "it gets done at the start of the month".
- No invoicing software was named. Payment appears to be by bank transfer and by card links, but the tool was not identified.
- Invoices go out "around the 3rd or 4th, sometimes later".
- Terms were not stated. Asked when parents are expected to pay, the answer was "when they get it".
- Chasing: happens by text if someone notices. No aged debt list exists.
- Disputes are common - parents query sessions they say were cancelled. There is no cancellation record to check against.
- Asked what is currently outstanding: not known.
- Asked how many parents pay late: not known.
- Discounts for siblings and for block bookings exist but the rules for them could not be stated consistently.

gold.trigger: The start of the month, when invoices are described as being done - 'around the 3rd or 4th, sometimes later'.

participants: Tutors, who keep the session logs

Sibling and block booking discount rules, which could not be stated consistently

bottlenecks_and_risks: Who compiles the invoices was not established, so no one is accountable for billing accuracy or timing

Payment terms were never stated; asked when parents are expected to pay, the answer was 'when they get it', so there is nothing to enforce

recommended_improved_process: Record sessions as delivered against the booking, in one system, for all tutors
Record cancellations with the notice given, so disputes can be resolved against a record
Publish written payment terms and discount rules
Name an owner for invoicing and set a fixed invoice date

input:
Discovery notes - dental practice, recall and reappointment

- Patients are recalled at 6 or 12 month intervals depending on risk.
- Practice manager (Julie) described the process: "Reception books the patient's next check-up before they leave the surgery. Everyone gets reappointed at the desk. That's the rule and it's been the rule for years."
- Part-time receptionist (Marie), separately: "Hardly anyone books at the desk - they say they'll ring. So on Tuesdays and Thursdays I work through a printed list of everyone due and ring them. That's how the book gets filled."
- Both accounts were given as the current process and neither was withdrawn when raised.
- The printed list is generated from SOE by Julie, monthly, and is worked through in name order.
- Marie is in two days a week. The list from the previous month is not always finished before the next one is printed.
- Where a patient is not reached, no further attempt is defined. Some are rung once, some three times.
- Nothing is recorded against the patient about the attempted contact.
- SOE can send SMS reminders for booked appointments; it is used for that but not for recall.
- Patients who have not attended for over two years remain on the list and are still rung.
- Failure-to-attend rate and recall conversion are not measured.

gold.objective: Recall patients for their six or twelve month check-up and fill the appointment book.
gold.trigger: Contradictory in input: Julie describes the trigger as the patient leaving the surgery, when reception reappoints them at the desk; Marie describes it as her Tuesday and Thursday sessions working through a printed list of patients due

participants: Julie, the practice manager, who generates the list
Marie, the part-time receptionist, two days a week

input:
Subject: rebooking - my fault I know

Hi Lucy,

You asked why our rebooking rate is poor. Here's what actually happens.

The intention is that every client rebooks at the till before they leave. Chloe on reception is supposed to ask. Sometimes she does, sometimes there's a queue and she doesn't, and the client's out the door.

Then the backup is meant to be that Chloe goes through Fresha, finds clients who haven't been in for eight or ten weeks, and texts them. She does this when she remembers, which is honestly about once a month, and only when the salon's quiet.

There's no list, she just scrolls. So she texts the same familiar names and the ones she doesn't know well never get contacted.

Fresha can send automated reminders for booked appointments and it does that fine. What it doesn't do - or we don't have it doing - is chase people who haven't rebooked.

Colour clients are the ones that matter because they're on a six week cycle and if you miss them they go somewhere else. I'd say we lose a couple a month that way.

Nobody measures any of this. I only noticed because takings were down.

Priya

gold.trigger: A client is at the till at the end of their appointment and should be asked to rebook; the fallback is Chloe scrolling Fresha for clients not seen for eight to ten weeks.

participants: Colour clients on a six week cycle

Subject: agency drivers

Peter,

You asked about how we get forklift drivers in. We use two agencies. When we're short - holidays, someone off sick, a big week - the warehouse manager rings whichever agency answers first and asks for a body for the morning.

They turn up at 6am. Someone on shift signs them in. In theory we check their licence before they get on a truck. In practice it depends who's on the gate. Milan always asks, one of the shift leaders never does, and if it's busy nobody does.

We don't take a copy. We don't record the number or the expiry. So if you asked me today whether every agency driver who's operated a truck here this year was licensed, I couldn't tell you.

There's also our own site familiarisation - the racking layout, the pedestrian routes, where the chargers are. That's supposed to be a walk round with a shift leader. It's usually "follow him and don't hit anything".

The agency say they check. I've never seen their evidence and it's not in our file.

We had a near miss in the spring, a pallet dropped near the pick face. The driver was agency. We didn't record it as an incident.

Steve

input:
NIGHTLY PRODUCE ORDERING
Kitchen procedure, restaurant

Fresh produce is ordered daily from a market trader for delivery the following morning.

Trigger: end of evening service. The cut-off for placing the order is 9pm.

Steps as currently performed:
1. The chef on duty walks the fridges and dry store and forms a view of what is needed.
2. The chef telephones the trader's number and leaves a voicemail listing the items and quantities.
3. No written copy of the order is retained.
4. The delivery arrives between 5am and 7am. It is left in the yard where there is no chilled storage. The kitchen opens at 8am.
5. The first chef in checks the delivery against the delivery note and puts it away.
6. Delivery notes are spiked. Invoices arrive weekly by post and are paid by the owner without matching to the notes.

Points recorded: because no order is retained, the delivery cannot be checked against what was asked for, only against what the trader says he sent. Different chefs order differently for the same expected covers - one orders to a par level in his head, another orders "a bit extra". Where the 9pm cut-off is missed the order is placed the next morning for the day after, and the kitchen substitutes from the freezer. Produce left in the yard has been rejected on temperature grounds twice. Price is not agreed in advance and varies week to week; nobody checks the rate charged against the market rate.

gold.objective: Order fresh produce daily from a market trader for next-morning delivery to the restaurant kitchen.
gold.trigger: The end of evening service, against a 9pm cut-off for placing the order.

participants: The first chef in the following morning, who checks the delivery
The owner, who pays the weekly invoices

inputs_data_required: What the chef sees walking the fridges and dry store
The chef's view of what is needed for expected covers
The delivery note
systems_involved: Telephone voicemail (the order is left as a voicemail; no written copy is retained)

Weekly posted invoices

bottlenecks_and_risks: No copy of the order is retained, so the delivery can only be checked against what the trader says he sent, not against what was actually asked for

Different chefs order differently for the same expected covers - one to a par level in his head, another 'a bit extra' - so cost and waste vary by who is on

input:
Discovery notes - lettings and management, tenant complaints

- Tenants complain about repairs not being done, about deposit deductions, and about the firm's own responsiveness.
- Route in: phone to the office, email to individual staff, and increasingly a message through the property portal listing site.
- There is no complaints procedure document, although the firm is a member of a redress scheme which requires one and requires a defined timescale.
- Handling: whoever takes the complaint tries to resolve it. If they cannot, it is passed to the branch manager (Ranjit), usually verbally.
- No log is kept. The firm cannot say how many complaints it received last year.
- The redress scheme requires a complaint to be escalated to them only after the firm's own process is exhausted or after 8 weeks. Three cases in the last year went straight to the scheme because the tenant was never told there was an internal process.
- The scheme has upheld two complaints and awarded compensation. The firm was unable to produce a file of correspondence in one of them; the evidence was spread across two staff members' Outlook accounts, one of whom had left.
- Nobody was named as responsible for complaints handling.
- Complaints are not discussed at the weekly branch meeting.
- No root cause work is done; the same issue (repairs not progressed) is behind most of them.

Subject: hours and the whiteboard

Hi,

You asked how we do the wages. Here it is.

There's a whiteboard in the stockroom with the week's rota on it. Names down the side, days across. When someone works a shift they're supposed to write their actual in and out times next to the rota'd ones, because they never match - people stay late for a delivery, or come in early for a stock take.

On Sunday I photograph the whiteboard on my phone before Kelly wipes it for the new week. Then I sit down and type the hours into a spreadsheet, one tab per month.

That spreadsheet goes to the accountant on the 20th and he does the payroll and the payslips.

What goes wrong: people don't write their actual times, they just leave the rota'd ones, so we underpay them and they come and tell me. Sometimes the board gets wiped before I photograph it and I'm reconstructing from memory. The Saturday temps aren't on the rota at all so I add them from what the supervisor tells me.

Holiday accrual - the accountant does something with it but I don't understand it and I don't check it.

There's no clocking system. The photo on my phone is the only record and I delete them when the phone fills up.

Marion

gold.trigger: Sunday, when the owner photographs the whiteboard before it is wiped for the new week.

participants: Kelly, who wipes the board for the new week
The supervisor, who reports Saturday temps' hours
Staff who write their actual times on the board

inputs_data_required: The whiteboard rota with rota'd hours and actual in and out times written next to them

FILING DEADLINES AND STATUTORY OBLIGATIONS
Extract from practice quality manual, and note of review

Manual, section 2.4: "A central deadline register is maintained on the practice management system recording, for every client, the due dates for accounts, corporation tax, self assessment, VAT, confirmation statements and payroll RTI. The register is reviewed weekly by the compliance partner, who circulates a report of items falling due within 30 days. No deadline may be tracked outside the register."

Note of review: the practice management system holds due dates but no report is run from it and no weekly review takes place. The compliance partner role has not been filled since the previous holder retired.

What is actually used is a wall planner in the partners' office, written up each January by the office manager, on which VAT quarters and the January self assessment deadline are marked. Individual partners keep their own lists for their own clients; two use Outlook tasks, one uses a notebook.

Both the manual and the wall planner were described by staff as "how we do it".

Further points: two late filing penalties were incurred last year, both for confirmation statements, which appear on neither the wall planner nor anyone's list. Clients who join mid-year are not added to the planner until the following January. Where a client is late providing records, the deadline is not re-flagged. Nobody could state how many clients have a deadline in the next 30 days.

gold.trigger: Contradictory in input: the manual specifies a weekly review of a central deadline register by the compliance partner; in practice the trigger is the office manager writing up a wall planner each January

Subject: corporate memberships

Hi,

You asked about the corporate deals. This is a sore point.

We sell corporate memberships to local employers - a block of memberships at a discount, or a discount code their staff can use individually.

I've told everyone the standard is 15% off the standard monthly rate for anything over ten members, and that anything bigger than that comes to me. That's the policy and I've said it in a team meeting.

What actually happens is the two sales staff negotiate whatever they like. Ryan did a deal with the call centre on the retail park at 30% with no minimum numbers and a free joining fee, and I only found out when the direct debits started coming through wrong. He says I approved it. I've got no memory of that and there's no email.

Kel does hers differently again - she throws in free guest passes instead of discounting, which I actually prefer, but it's not written anywhere either.

There's no quote document. It's an email, or sometimes just a conversation at the company's reception desk.

We don't know what a corporate member is worth compared to a normal one, or whether the discounted ones stay longer or leave sooner.

Nothing's in Legend except the member records once they join.

gold.objective: Quote corporate memberships to local employers - blocks of memberships at a discount, or a discount code for staff.
gold.trigger: An employer enquiry, handled by a salesperson, sometimes in conversation at the company's reception desk.

owner_and_participants.owner: Contradictory in input: the writer states the policy is 15% off for over ten members with anything larger coming to him, and that he said so in a team meeting; Ryan agreed a 30% deal with no minimum numbers and a free joining fee and says the writer approved it, which the writer has no memory of and for which there is no email

inputs_data_required: The employer's requirements
The standard monthly rate and the stated 15% policy
systems_involved: Legend (holds member records once staff join; nothing about the corporate deal)
Email and in-person conversation (how quotes are given)
current_process: An employer enquiry arises and a salesperson handles it
The stated policy is 15% off the standard monthly rate for over ten members, with anything bigger referred to the writer
In practice the two sales staff negotiate what they like - Ryan agreed 30% with no minimum numbers and a free joining fee; Kel gives free guest passes instead of discounting
The deal is communicated by email or in conversation at the company's reception desk; there is no quote document
Members join and their records appear in Legend
bottlenecks_and_risks: Whether the 30% deal was approved is contradictory and unresolvable - Ryan says the writer approved it, the writer has no memory of it and there is no email - so authority cannot be established after the fact
The 15% policy was communicated verbally in a team meeting and is not written down, so it cannot be enforced
The discrepancy was discovered only when direct debits started coming through wrong, meaning the club was already committed
Kel's approach of giving free guest passes is preferred by the writer but is also unwritten, so a second undocumented practice exists
There is no quote document at all - just an email or a conversation - so what was agreed is disputable
The club does not know what a corporate member is worth compared with a standard member, or whether discounted members stay longer or leave sooner, so the discounting has no evidence base
Nothing about the corporate deal is held in Legend, only the member records once they join
recommended_improved_process: Write down and publish the corporate pricing policy including discount bands and minimum numbers
Require a quote document for every corporate deal, recording the terms offered
Set an approval threshold above which the manager must approve in writing before the offer is made
Record the corporate agreement and its terms against the member records in Legend
Standardise the non-discount alternatives such as guest passes
Measure corporate member value and retention against standard members
Review live corporate deals against the policy and renegotiate where necessary

An AI agent can flag live corporate deals whose terms fall outside the published policy, such as the 30% arrangement
An AI agent can report corporate member value and retention against standard members
human_approvals_controls: The manager approves in writing any quote outside the published discount bands, before it is offered
The salesperson issues only the approved quote document; verbal terms are not binding
The owner approves the published corporate pricing policy and any change to it
Renegotiating or honouring an out-of-policy live deal is a management decision

Subject: merchant credits

Hi,

Something I've realised and I'm not proud of.

When we do a job we buy the parts on the merchant account and charge them on to the customer at cost plus a bit. Standard.

What happens when we buy the wrong part, or over-order, is the lad takes it back to the merchant and they credit our account. That credit sits on our account and reduces what we pay them at the end of the month.

The customer has already been invoiced for the parts as originally bought. Nobody goes back and adjusts the customer's invoice. So we've been paid for parts that went back.

It's not deliberate. There's no link between the merchant credit note and the job it came from. The credits show as a line on the monthly statement with a reference that means nothing to me.

I noticed because a customer queried a bill and I went and looked, and the £180 of copper we charged her for had gone back to City Plumbing three days later.

I don't know how much this adds up to. It could be a few hundred a year or it could be thousands.

Amy does the invoicing in QuickBooks from the job sheets. The merchant statement doesn't go anywhere near her, it comes to me.

Gareth

Amy, who invoices in QuickBooks from job sheets

Merchant trade accounts and their monthly statements

Where the wrong part is bought or too many are ordered, the engineer takes them back and the merchant credits the account
The credit reduces what the firm pays the merchant at the end of the month
Amy invoices the customer in QuickBooks from the job sheets, based on the parts as originally bought
Nobody goes back to adjust the customer's invoice
The merchant statement comes to Gareth and does not go near Amy
bottlenecks_and_risks: Customers are charged for parts that were returned to the merchant - identified when a customer queried a bill and £180 of copper had gone back to City Plumbing three days later
There is no link between a merchant credit note and the job it came from, so the credit cannot be traced back even deliberately
Credit lines appear on the statement with references that mean nothing to the owner
The merchant statement goes to Gareth and the invoicing is done by Amy from job sheets, so the two halves of the information never meet

This is a customer-facing billing error, so the risk is reputational and potentially a consumer law issue, not just internal
recommended_improved_process: Require a job reference on every merchant purchase and on every return, so credits can be traced to the job
Route the merchant statement to whoever raises invoices, not only to the owner
Reconcile merchant purchases and credits to jobs before the customer invoice is raised

Quantify the historic exposure and decide how to put affected customers right
Report monthly on credits received and credits passed through to customers
